lessons.title: Gaussian mixture models and the EM algorithm

blocks.md:
## Why this matters

K-means gives every point exactly one cluster and assumes round clusters. Real groups overlap and are stretched: a customer can be 70% "bargain hunter" and 30% "loyal regular", and a cloud of points can be a tilted ellipse. A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) describes the data as a blend of normal distributions, gives each point a **probability** of belonging to each cluster, and learns elliptical shapes. It is also your first encounter with the EM algorithm, a general method used far beyond clustering.

## The model

A GMM with K components says each data point was generated in two steps: first pick a component k with probability πₖ (the **mixing weights**, which sum to 1), then draw the point from that component's normal distribution with mean μₖ and covariance matrix Σₖ. The resulting density is a weighted sum of bells:

$$
p(x) = Σ_k π_k · N(x | μ_k, Σ_k)
$$

N(x | μ, Σ) is the **multivariate normal density** from the handbook: in d dimensions,

$$
N(x | μ, Σ) = exp(−½ (x − μ)ᵀ Σ⁻¹ (x − μ)) / √((2π)^d · det(Σ))
$$

(x − μ)ᵀ Σ⁻¹ (x − μ) is a squared distance from the mean that takes the shape of the cloud into account (the Mahalanobis distance), Σ⁻¹ is the inverse of the covariance matrix and det(Σ) its determinant. In one dimension it reduces to the familiar bell with variance σ². The covariance matrix sets each component's shape: its diagonal holds variances (spread along each axis), its off-diagonal entries the covariances (tilt).

Which component generated each point is unknown: a **latent** (hidden) variable. If we knew it, fitting would be easy (compute each group's share, mean and covariance). If we knew the parameters, guessing the component would be easy (Bayes' theorem). EM alternates between the two.

## The EM algorithm

Start from initial parameters (sklearn initialises with k-means), then repeat:

**E-step** (expectation): for every point n and component k compute the **responsibility**, the posterior probability that component k generated xₙ:

$$
r_nk = π_k N(x_n | μ_k, Σ_k) / Σ_j π_j N(x_n | μ_j, Σ_j)
$$

This is Bayes' theorem: prior πₖ times likelihood, divided by the total. Each row of the responsibility matrix sums to 1.

**M-step** (maximisation): refit each component as a weighted average, with the responsibilities as weights. Let Nₖ = Σₙ rₙₖ, the "effective number of points" in component k:

$$
μ_k = (1 / N_k) Σ_n r_nk x_n
Σ_k = (1 / N_k) Σ_n r_nk (x_n − μ_k)(x_n − μ_k)ᵀ
π_k = N_k / N
$$

where N is the number of points. Each iteration never decreases the **log-likelihood** Σₙ log p(xₙ), and the loop stops when it improves by less than a tolerance (`tol`, default 0.001) or after `max_iter` iterations (default 100). Like k-means, EM finds a local optimum, so `n_init` restarts help.

### Worked example in one dimension

Data: 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9. Two components with π = (0.5, 0.5), means 2 and 8, variances 1 and 1.

**E-step for x = 5**: it is 3 away from both means with equal variances and weights, so r = (0.5, 0.5). For x = 4 (not in our data) the densities would be N(4 | 2, 1) = 0.054 and N(4 | 8, 1) ≈ 0.0001, giving responsibilities 0.9975 and 0.0025. Points 1, 2, 3 belong to component 1 with responsibility essentially 1, and 7, 8, 9 to component 2.

**M-step for component 1**: N₁ = 1 + 1 + 1 + 0.5 + (almost 0 three times) = 3.5, so π₁ = 3.5/7 = 0.5. The mean is (1 + 2 + 3 + 0.5 × 5)/3.5 = 8.5/3.5 ≈ 2.4286: half of point 5 pulled it up from 2. The variance is the responsibility-weighted mean squared distance from 2.4286, ≈ 1.6735.

Responsibilities depend on more than distance. With weights (0.8, 0.2) instead, x = 5 gets responsibility 0.8 for component 1. With the second component's variance raised to 4, x = 5 goes 0.94 to the wider component 2: a wide bell reaches further. Your drill `d-estep` performs a full E-step and M-step.

## GMM versus k-means

K-means is a special, "hard" case: if every component has the same spherical covariance σ²I that shrinks toward 0, the responsibilities become 0 or 1 (nearest mean wins) and the M-step for μ becomes the centroid update. GMM adds:

- **soft assignments**: `predict_proba` returns the responsibilities; points with no responsibility above, say, 0.9 are genuinely ambiguous (6 of 400 in the example below);
- **elliptical clusters** of different sizes and orientations;
- a **density** estimate: `score_samples(X)` returns log p(x), and very low values flag anomalies.

The handbook's stretched-blobs example (`make_blobs(400, centers=4, cluster_std=0.6, random_state=0)`, axes flipped, multiplied by a random 2 × 2 matrix from seed 13) makes this concrete. Agreement with the true groups (adjusted Rand index, 1 = perfect):

| model | ARI |
|---|---|
| KMeans(4) | 0.813 |
| GMM, covariance_type="spherical" | 0.803 |
| GMM, "diag" | 0.852 |
| GMM, "full" | 0.987 |

## Covariance types

`covariance_type` controls the shape freedom, and so the number of parameters:

- `"full"` (**the default**; the handbook says the default is "diag", which is incorrect): each component has its own unrestricted covariance, an ellipse with any orientation.
- `"tied"`: all components share one full covariance.
- `"diag"`: axis-aligned ellipses (only variances, no covariances).
- `"spherical"`: circles, one variance per component, closest to k-means.

More freedom fits better but needs more data and can overfit; in high dimensions a full covariance has d(d + 1)/2 numbers per component.

## Choosing the number of components

Because a GMM is a probability model, you can use information criteria that reward likelihood and penalise parameters: **BIC** (Bayesian information criterion) and **AIC**. Lower is better. For the stretched blobs with full covariances:

| K | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BIC | 2319.7 | 2050.3 | 1867.8 | 1672.6 | 1697.8 | 1720.0 | 1752.5 |

The minimum is at K = 4, the true number of groups. The silhouette score works too, on the hard labels from `predict`.

```
from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture

gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=4, covariance_type="full", n_init=5, random_state=42).fit(X)
labels = gmm.predict(X)            # most responsible component
probs = gmm.predict_proba(X)       # responsibilities, shape (n_samples, n_components)
gmm.weights_, gmm.means_, gmm.covariances_
gmm.bic(X)
```

Scale features first when their units differ, as for k-means.

## Reading the handbook's GMM class

The from-scratch class follows the formulas above with three issues worth knowing before you copy it for homework. First, it updates each covariance with `np.cov(X.T, aweights=r[:, k], ddof=0)` and then divides by Nₖ again; `np.cov` with `aweights` already divides by the sum of the weights, so the covariances shrink every iteration. Drop the extra `1/N[k]`. Second, `predict` picks the component with the highest density N(x | μₖ, Σₖ) and ignores the weights πₖ; the posterior uses πₖ N(·). Third, it initialises by splitting the rows into consecutive chunks with `np.array_split`, so the result depends on the row order; shuffle first, or start from k-means as sklearn does. (The attribute is also spelled `n_componets` throughout; consistent, so it works.)

## Common mistakes

> **Reading `predict` as certain.** Check `predict_proba` for points near boundaries.

> **Using full covariances with few points per component.** Covariance matrices can become singular; use `"diag"` or raise `reg_covar`.

> **Forgetting it is a local optimum.** Use `n_init` > 1.

## Summary

A GMM models data as p(x) = Σ πₖ N(x | μₖ, Σₖ). EM alternates the E-step (responsibilities rₙₖ ∝ πₖ N(xₙ | μₖ, Σₖ), rows summing to 1) and the M-step (Nₖ = Σ rₙₖ; weighted means and covariances; πₖ = Nₖ/N), never decreasing the log-likelihood. It gives soft assignments, elliptical clusters and densities; k-means is its hard, spherical limit. sklearn's default covariance_type is "full"; choose K with BIC.

blocks.q:
A point has densities 0.05 under component 1 and 0.20 under component 2, with weights π = (0.8, 0.2). What is its responsibility for component 1? Type a decimal.
```python
a, b = 0.8 * 0.05, 0.2 * 0.20
print(round(a / (a + b), 4))
```
blocks.why: 0.04 versus 0.04: the larger weight of component 1 exactly offsets its lower density.

blocks.q: What does the M-step of EM compute?
options: The responsibility of each component for each point
New weights, means and covariances, as averages weighted by the responsibilities
blocks.why: The E-step computes responsibilities; the M-step uses them as weights to refit each Gaussian.

blocks.q:
After an E-step, component 1 has responsibilities 1, 1, 0.5 and 0 for the points 2, 4, 6 and 10. What is its new mean?
```python
r = [1, 1, 0.5, 0]
x = [2, 4, 6, 10]
print(sum(a * b for a, b in zip(r, x)) / sum(r))
```
blocks.why: (2 + 4 + 3)/2.5 = 9/2.5. Nₖ = 2.5 is the effective number of points.

blocks.q: How is k-means related to a GMM?
options: A GMM is k-means with more iterations
K-means is the limit of a GMM with equal spherical covariances shrinking to zero, which makes assignments hard
K-means is a GMM with full covariances
blocks.why: Equal tiny spherical variances make the nearest mean take responsibility 1, and the mean update becomes the centroid update.

blocks.q: Write `normal(x, mu, var)` (the 1-D normal density) and `responsibilities(x, pi, mu, var)` returning the list of posteriors for one point, rounded to 4. Use `math.exp`, `math.sqrt` and `math.pi`.
blocks.why: The last test: the wider component 2 takes x = 5 even though both means are 3 away, because its bell is still high there while component 1's has fallen off.

blocks.q: sklearn's `GaussianMixture` uses which covariance_type by default?
blocks.why: The handbook says "diag", but the default is "full", each component with its own unrestricted covariance.

blocks.q: From memory, explain the E-step and the M-step of EM for a Gaussian mixture, and give two things a GMM can do that k-means cannot.
blocks.model: In the E-step, for every point and component we compute the responsibility: the component's weight times its normal density at the point, divided by the same quantity summed over all components, so each point gets probabilities that sum to 1. In the M-step we refit every component using the responsibilities as weights: Nₖ is the sum of its responsibilities, the new mean is the responsibility-weighted mean of the points, the covariance the weighted average of the outer products of deviations, and the weight is Nₖ/N. Repeating never lowers the likelihood. Unlike k-means, a GMM gives soft membership probabilities and can model elliptical clusters with different sizes and orientations; it also gives a density, useful for anomaly detection, and BIC for choosing K.
blocks.rubric: Check that you mentioned weights πₖ in the E-step and Nₖ in the M-step.

cards.q: Write the GMM density.
cards.a: p(x) = Σₖ πₖ N(x | μₖ, Σₖ), with the weights πₖ summing to 1.

cards.q: Write the responsibility formula.
cards.a: rₙₖ = πₖ N(xₙ | μₖ, Σₖ) / Σⱼ πⱼ N(xₙ | μⱼ, Σⱼ).

cards.q: Give the M-step updates.
cards.a: Nₖ = Σₙ rₙₖ; μₖ = Σₙ rₙₖ xₙ / Nₖ; Σₖ = Σₙ rₙₖ (xₙ − μₖ)(xₙ − μₖ)ᵀ / Nₖ; πₖ = Nₖ / N.

cards.q: How do you choose the number of components in a GMM?
cards.a: Fit several K and pick the lowest BIC (or AIC); silhouette also works on hard labels.

blocks.md:
## Why this matters

Almost every Sigmoid homework ends in a plot: accuracy against a hyperparameter, a decision boundary, a silhouette plot, missing values per column. A plot is often the fastest way to spot a skewed feature, an outlier, a leaking column or an overfitting curve, and it is how your conclusions are read by others. This lesson covers how matplotlib is organised, which chart answers which question, the seaborn shortcuts from the handbook, and the habits that make a plot readable.

## How matplotlib is organised

A **Figure** is the whole image (the canvas). It contains one or more **Axes**: each Axes is one plot area with its own x-axis, y-axis, title and data. (Axes is not the plural of axis; an Axes has two axis objects.) Everything you draw goes onto an Axes.

matplotlib has two interfaces, and the handbook shows both:

- **pyplot / MATLAB style**: `plt.plot(...)`, `plt.title(...)` act on the "current" Axes, which pyplot tracks for you. `plt.subplot(2, 1, 1)` means "a grid of 2 rows and 1 column, make panel 1 current".
- **Object-oriented style**: create the objects and call methods on them.

```
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)                 # 100 evenly spaced points from 0 to 10
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6, 5))   # a Figure and an array of 2 Axes
ax[0].plot(x, np.sin(x), color="red", label="sin(x)")
ax[1].plot(x, np.cos(x), linestyle="dotted", label="cos(x)")
ax[0].set_title("Sine")                     # object style: set_title, set_xlabel, set_xlim
ax[1].set_xlabel("x")
for a in ax:
    a.legend()
fig.tight_layout()                          # stop labels overlapping
fig.savefig("waves.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
```

Prefer the object style for anything with more than one panel: it is explicit about which Axes you are drawing on. Note the naming difference: `plt.title` and `plt.xlim` versus `ax.set_title` and `ax.set_xlim`. `plt.subplots(2, 2)` returns a 2 × 2 array, so you index it as `ax[0, 1]`; `ax.flat` loops over all panels.

## Which chart for which question

| Question | Chart | matplotlib | seaborn |
|---|---|---|---|
| How does y change with x (ordered x)? | line | `ax.plot` | `sns.lineplot` |
| How are two numeric variables related? | scatter | `ax.scatter` | `sns.scatterplot`, `sns.jointplot` |
| What is the distribution of one variable? | histogram, KDE | `ax.hist` | `sns.histplot`, `sns.kdeplot` |
| How do distributions compare across groups? | box, violin | `ax.boxplot` | `sns.boxplot`, `sns.violinplot` |
| How large is each category? | bar | `ax.bar`, `ax.barh` | `sns.barplot`, `sns.countplot` |
| How do many variables correlate? | heatmap | `ax.imshow` | `sns.heatmap(df.corr(), annot=True)` |
| How does a function of two variables look? | contour | `ax.contour`, `ax.contourf` | |
| How uncertain is each measurement? | error bars | `ax.errorbar` | built into `barplot`, `lineplot` |

### Line and scatter

`ax.plot(x, y)` connects points in order, so use it when x is ordered (time, a hyperparameter). `ax.scatter(x, y, c=values, s=sizes, alpha=0.3, cmap="viridis")` can give every point its own colour (`c`) and size (`s`, in points squared), which encodes extra variables; `alpha` (0 to 1) sets transparency so dense regions show. Add `fig.colorbar(...)` to explain a colour scale. For many thousands of identical-looking points, `ax.plot(x, y, "o")` is faster than `scatter`, because scatter styles each point individually.

### Histograms

A histogram divides the range from the minimum to the maximum into equal-width **bins** and counts the values in each. Each bin includes its left edge and excludes its right edge, except the last bin, which includes both. For the values 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 10 with `bins=3`, the edges are 1, 4, 7, 10 and the counts 6, 3, 1. The number of bins changes the story: too few hide structure (two peaks merge), too many show noise. `ax.hist` returns `(counts, edges, patches)`, so you can check the numbers behind the picture. `density=True` rescales the bars so their total area is 1, which lets you compare groups of different sizes. `ax.hist2d(x, y, bins=30)` counts points in a grid of 2-D bins.

### KDE

A **kernel density estimate** places a small smooth bump (usually a normal curve) on every observation and adds them up, giving a smooth version of a histogram. The bump width (`bw_adjust` in seaborn) plays the role of the bin width. The handbook's KDE example compares the age distributions of heart patients with and without disease. It uses `shade=True`, which seaborn has deprecated; write `fill=True`.

### Box plots and violin plots

A **box plot** summarises a distribution with five numbers: the box runs from the first quartile Q1 (25th percentile) to the third quartile Q3 (75th), with a line at the median. The whiskers reach the most extreme data points within 1.5 × IQR of the box, where IQR = Q3 − Q1 is the interquartile range, and points beyond the whiskers are drawn individually as potential outliers. (Week 9 turns this rule into an outlier detector.) A **violin plot** draws a mirrored KDE around a slim box plot, so it also shows shape, for example two peaks, which a box hides.

```
import seaborn as sns
sns.boxplot(data=df, x="target", y="age")       # one box per class
sns.violinplot(data=df, x="target", y="age")
sns.jointplot(data=df, x="age", y="trestbps", kind="hex")   # scatter/hexbin with marginal histograms
sns.lmplot(data=df, x="age", y="chol", hue="target")        # scatter + a regression line per class
```

seaborn functions take a DataFrame and column names, map a categorical column to colour with `hue=`, and draw on matplotlib Axes. Axes-level functions (`boxplot`, `histplot`, `kdeplot`, `scatterplot`) accept `ax=` so they fit in your subplot grid; figure-level functions (`jointplot`, `lmplot`, `pairplot`, `relplot`) create their own Figure and take `height=` instead.

### Error bars and contours

`ax.errorbar(x, y, yerr=dy, fmt=".k")` draws each point with a vertical bar of ± dy; `fmt` uses the same shorthand as `plot` (`.` marker, `k` black). Use it for the mean ± standard deviation of cross-validation scores at each hyperparameter value: it shows whether a difference is bigger than the noise.

`ax.contourf(X, Y, Z)` colours regions of a 2-D grid by the value Z. Decision boundary plots are made this way: build a grid with `np.meshgrid`, predict on every grid point, and draw the predictions with `contourf` (sklearn's `DecisionBoundaryDisplay` does it for you).

## Habits of a readable plot

- Every axis has a label with units; every plot has a title that says what it shows.
- One message per plot. If the reader must compare panels, share axes (`plt.subplots(..., sharey=True)`).
- Use a legend only when there is more than one series, and put the key fact in the title ("Test accuracy peaks at max_depth = 4").
- Use colour to encode a variable, not to decorate. Sequential maps (`viridis`) for ordered values, a diverging map (`coolwarm`) for correlations centred at 0, distinct hues for categories. Avoid red-green as the only distinction.
- Start bar charts at zero; line plots may zoom.
- Avoid 3-D effects and pie charts with many slices.
- Show uncertainty (error bars, shaded bands) when comparing models.

## Version notes for the handbook's code

- `plt.style.use("seaborn-whitegrid")` fails on matplotlib 3.6 and later; the style is now called `"seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid"`, or use `sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")`.
- `sns.kdeplot(..., shade=True)`: use `fill=True`.
- `%matplotlib inline` is only needed in old Jupyter versions; plots show automatically now. In a script, call `plt.show()`.

## Common mistakes

> **Mixing the two interfaces** (`plt.title` after creating `ax` objects can title the wrong panel). Use `ax.set_title`.

> **Reading a histogram without checking bins.** Try two or three bin counts before drawing conclusions.

> **Plots without labels.** A curve called "Figure 1" with unlabelled axes cannot be graded or understood.

## Summary

A Figure holds Axes; draw on Axes with methods (`ax.plot`, `ax.set_title`). Pick the chart from the question: line for ordered x, scatter for relationships, histogram or KDE for one distribution, box or violin to compare groups, heatmap for correlations, error bars for uncertainty. Histograms use equal-width bins from min to max. A box shows Q1, median, Q3 and whiskers to 1.5 × IQR. seaborn draws statistical plots from DataFrames with `x=`, `y=`, `hue=`.

blocks.q: `fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3)`. What is `ax`?
options: A 2 × 3 array of Axes objects, indexed like `ax[1, 2]`
blocks.why: subplots returns the Figure and an array of Axes with the grid's shape.

blocks.q:
Using numpy's rules (equal-width bins from min to max, last bin closed), what are the counts for the values 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 10 with 4 bins? Type them as a list.
```python
import numpy as np
counts, edges = np.histogram([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 10], bins=4)
print(counts.tolist())
```
blocks.why: The edges are 1, 3.25, 5.5, 7.75, 10. The empty third bin shows how one far value (10) stretches the range.

blocks.q: You want to compare the distribution of cholesterol between patients with and without heart disease, including whether either group has two peaks. Which plot fits best?
options: A line plot of cholesterol by row number
A violin plot (or overlaid KDEs) by target class
A bar chart of mean cholesterol per class
blocks.why: A violin shows each group's full distribution shape. A bar of means hides spread and shape; a box hides multiple peaks.

blocks.q: In a box plot, which points are drawn individually beyond the whiskers?
options: Points more than 1.5 × IQR below Q1 or above Q3
Points more than 3 standard deviations from the mean
blocks.why: The whiskers stop at the furthest data point within 1.5 × IQR of the box; anything further is plotted as a potential outlier.

blocks.q: Write `hist_counts(xs, bins)` that reproduces `np.histogram`'s counts: edges equally spaced from min(xs) to max(xs); a value belongs to bin i if edge[i] ≤ x < edge[i+1], except that the maximum goes in the last bin. Return the list of counts. Then `five_numbers(xs)` returning (min, Q1, median, Q3, max) using the same linear interpolation as `np.percentile` (position p·(n − 1) in the sorted list).
blocks.why: Q1 = 2.25 sits a quarter of the way between the 3rd and 4th sorted values (2 and 3): position 0.25 × 9 = 2.25. With IQR = 1.75, the upper whisker limit is 4 + 2.625 = 6.625, so 10 would be drawn as an outlier.


blocks.q: From memory, describe how you would visually compare a single hyperparameter's effect on train and validation accuracy, including how you would show the noise, and which labels and title the plot needs.
blocks.model: I would put the hyperparameter values on the x-axis (log scale for values like C) and plot two lines with ax.plot: mean training accuracy and mean cross-validation accuracy at each value. To show noise I would use ax.errorbar or ax.fill_between with the mean plus and minus the standard deviation of the fold scores. Labels: the hyperparameter's name on x, "accuracy" on y, a legend for train and validation, and a title stating the finding, such as "Validation accuracy peaks at max_depth = 4". The gap between the lines shows overfitting.
blocks.rubric: Check that you included uncertainty and a title that states the conclusion.

cards.q: What is the difference between a Figure and an Axes?
cards.a: A Figure is the whole image; an Axes is one plot area inside it with its own x and y axis.

cards.q: What does a box plot show?
cards.a: Q1, median and Q3 as the box; whiskers to the furthest points within 1.5 × IQR; points beyond as possible outliers.

cards.q: Which plot for the distribution of one numeric variable, and which to compare it across groups?
cards.a: Histogram or KDE; box or violin plot (or overlaid KDEs) by group.

cards.a: ax.set_title("..."), likewise ax.set_xlabel, ax.set_xlim.

lessons.sub: About 30 min reading · Handbook chapter 16 · Homework 14
lessons.title: Outliers: detecting and deciding what to do

blocks.md:
## Why this matters

An **outlier** is an observation that differs markedly from the rest: a 45-year-old in a list of teenagers' ages, a house priced at 100 times the median, a sensor reading of −999. Some are errors, some are rare but real, and some are exactly what you are looking for (fraud, faults). They matter because many models and statistics are sensitive to them: one extreme value moves a mean, a variance, a linear regression line and a k-means centroid. Homework 14 has you run four sklearn detectors on the same data, compare which points each flags, and measure how removing them changes a regression. This lesson explains how each detector thinks, so the differences make sense.

## First: what kind of outlier?

Before removing anything, ask where the value came from.

- **Errors** (typos, unit mix-ups, placeholder codes such as 999, broken sensors): fix them if you can, otherwise treat them as missing.
- **Rare but genuine** values (a billionaire's income): they belong to the population. Removing them makes the model wrong for such cases; robust methods or transformations (log, Box-Cox next lesson) are often better than deletion.
- **The signal itself** (fraud, intrusion, machine failure): this is **anomaly detection**, and the outliers are what you want to find, not remove.

Also distinguish **training-time cleaning** (remove outliers from the training set so they do not distort the fit) from **prediction time** (new data may still contain them, as the handbook's conclusion warns). Only ever decide on removal using the training data, never the test set.

## Univariate rules

### z-score

z = (x − mean)/std counts how many standard deviations a value is from the mean; |z| > 3 is a common cut-off. It has a weakness called **masking**: the outlier inflates the mean and the standard deviation that are supposed to expose it. For the ages 12, 13, 14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 45: the mean is 18.4, the standard deviation (dividing by n) 9.10, and the 45 has z = 2.92, below 3. The rule misses the obvious outlier.

### The box-plot (IQR) rule

Robust statistics are barely affected by extreme values. The **interquartile range** IQR = Q3 − Q1 measures the spread of the middle half of the data, and the box-plot rule (Tukey's fences) flags values outside:

$$
[Q1 − 1.5 · IQR,  Q3 + 1.5 · IQR]
$$

For the same ages, numpy's default percentiles give Q1 = 14.25 and Q3 = 17.75, so IQR = 3.5 and the fences are 9.0 and 23.0. The 45 is flagged; the others are not. This is the "dots beyond the whiskers" in a box plot, the handbook's last method, and your drill `d-iqr`. Using 3 instead of 1.5 flags only "far out" values.

Univariate rules check one column at a time. A 2-metre-tall person and a 40-kilogram person are each plausible; a 2-metre person weighing 40 kg is an outlier only in the combination. That is what the multivariate detectors are for.

## The four sklearn detectors

All four follow the same interface: `fit_predict(X)` returns **+1 for inliers and −1 for outliers**; `decision_function` or `score_samples` gives a continuous score (lower means more abnormal). Their `contamination` (or `nu`) parameter is your guess of the outlier share, and it directly sets how many points get flagged.

### Isolation Forest

Build many random trees: each split picks a random feature and a random threshold between that feature's min and max. Keep splitting until every point is alone. An outlier, being few and different, gets **isolated in few splits** (a short path from the root); a normal point in a dense region needs many. The anomaly score comes from the average path length over the trees. It is fast, works in high dimensions and needs no scaling. Default `contamination="auto"`.

### Elliptic Envelope

Assume the inliers come from one multivariate normal distribution. Fit its mean and covariance **robustly** (the Minimum Covariance Determinant estimator, which ignores the most extreme points while fitting), then flag points with a large Mahalanobis distance, that is, outside the fitted ellipse. Good for roughly Gaussian, single-cluster data; poor for several clusters or curved shapes. Default `contamination=0.1`.

### Local Outlier Factor

Compare each point's local density with that of its k nearest neighbours (`n_neighbors=20` by default). A point in a sparse spot surrounded by dense neighbours has a **LOF** well above 1 and is an outlier; points in uniformly dense or uniformly sparse regions have LOF around 1. Because it is local, it finds outliers next to dense clusters that a global rule misses. sklearn stores the negated value in `negative_outlier_factor_`, so there **lower** means more outlying. It uses distances, so scale first; and as the handbook notes, distances become less informative as the number of features grows (the curse of dimensionality).

### One-Class SVM

Learn a boundary that encloses most of the data in kernel space (RBF by default), treating everything outside as an outlier. `nu` is an upper bound on the share of training points outside the boundary, and **its default is 0.5**, not 0.1 as the handbook says: with defaults, One-Class SVM flags about half of your data. Always set `nu` (and scale features, as for any SVM).

### On the same data

205 points: 200 drawn from a standard 2-D normal, plus 5 planted far away ((6, 6), (−5, 5), (7, −6), (0, 8), (5, 0)). With `contamination=0.05` (or `nu=0.05`):

| detector | points flagged | planted points caught |
|---|---|---|
| IsolationForest | 11 | 5 of 5 |
| EllipticEnvelope | 11 | 5 of 5 |
| LocalOutlierFactor | 11 | 5 of 5 |
| OneClassSVM (gamma="auto") | 16 | 3 of 5 |

With their defaults the counts change completely: IsolationForest flags 21, EllipticEnvelope 21 and One-Class SVM 102. The contamination setting decides how many; the method decides which. That is why homework 14 asks you to plot the number of outliers against contamination.

## Removing flagged rows correctly

The handbook's pattern `df["outlier"] = pd.Series(model.fit_predict(df.values))` has a trap: a new Series gets the index 0, 1, 2, …, and assigning it to a DataFrame aligns by index. If `df` was filtered or shuffled earlier, rows get the wrong labels (or NaN). Assign the array directly:

```
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest

iso = IsolationForest(contamination=0.02, random_state=0)
mask = iso.fit_predict(X_train) == 1          # True for inliers
X_train_clean, y_train_clean = X_train[mask], y_train[mask]
print((~mask).sum(), "rows removed")
```

Then compare the model trained on all rows and on clean rows **on the same untouched test set**, which is exactly homework 14's last part. Expect linear regression to change more than a tree or KNN: squared error lets single far points pull the line.

### Alternatives to deletion

- **Capping** (winsorising): clip values to the fences or to the 1st/99th percentiles (`s.clip(lower, upper)`).
- **Transforming**: a log or Box-Cox transform shrinks long tails.
- **Robust models and losses**: `HuberRegressor`, median-based statistics, trees (which split on order, not distance).
- **RobustScaler**: scales with the median and IQR instead of mean and standard deviation.

## Common mistakes

> **Deleting outliers from the test set.** It makes the reported score optimistic.

> **Leaving One-Class SVM's nu at 0.5.** Half the data disappears.

> **Trusting z > 3 on small samples.** The outlier masks itself; use the IQR rule or robust z-scores.

## Summary

Decide first whether an outlier is an error, a rare real value or the target of interest. The z-score rule suffers from masking; the IQR rule flags values beyond Q1 − 1.5·IQR and Q3 + 1.5·IQR. Isolation Forest isolates anomalies in few random splits; Elliptic Envelope fits a robust Gaussian ellipse; Local Outlier Factor compares local density with neighbours; One-Class SVM learns a boundary around the data (set nu; the default is 0.5). All return −1 for outliers. contamination decides how many points are flagged. Clean only the training set, and compare models on the same test set.

blocks.q:
For the ages 12, 13, 14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 45, what are the IQR fences (Q1 − 1.5·IQR, Q3 + 1.5·IQR), using numpy's default percentiles? Type them separated by a space.
```python
import numpy as np
q1, q3 = np.percentile([12, 13, 14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 45], [25, 75])
iqr = q3 - q1
print(q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr)
```
blocks.why: Q1 = 14.25, Q3 = 17.75, IQR = 3.5. The 45 is outside; its z-score is only 2.92 because it inflates the standard deviation (masking).

blocks.q: What does `fit_predict` of sklearn's outlier detectors return?
options: The anomaly score of each point
blocks.why: Keep the rows where the result equals 1.

blocks.q: How does Isolation Forest decide that a point is an outlier?
options: It is far from the mean in standard deviations
Random splits isolate it after only a few cuts, so its average path length is short
Its local density is lower than its neighbours'
It lies outside a fitted ellipse
blocks.why: Few, different points are separated quickly by random thresholds; points in dense regions need many cuts.

blocks.q: You run `OneClassSVM(gamma="auto").fit_predict(X)` on 205 points and 102 are flagged. Why?
options: nu defaults to 0.5, allowing up to about half the points outside the boundary
blocks.why: Set nu to your expected outlier share, for example 0.05.

blocks.q: Write `zscores(xs)` returning the list of z-scores rounded to 2 (population standard deviation), and `fences(xs, k)` returning `(lower, upper)` = (Q1 − k·IQR, Q3 + k·IQR) rounded to 3, with numpy-style linear interpolation for the quartiles. Then `flag(xs, k)` returning the sorted values outside the fences.
blocks.why: The z-score of 45 stays under 3, while the IQR rule flags it. With k = 3 the fences widen to 3.75 and 28.25, and 45 is still out.

blocks.q: After removing outliers with Isolation Forest, how should you compare the models trained with and without them?
options: Remove outliers from the test set too, then compare
Evaluate both models on the same untouched test set
Compare the number of removed rows
blocks.why: Cleaning the test set changes the question being answered and inflates scores.

blocks.q: From memory, explain the masking problem of the z-score rule and why the IQR rule avoids it; then describe one situation where you should not remove outliers.
blocks.model: The z-score uses the mean and standard deviation, but an extreme value pulls the mean toward itself and inflates the standard deviation, so its own z-score shrinks and it can fall under the cut-off of 3: the outlier hides itself. The IQR rule uses the first and third quartiles, which depend on the middle of the data and barely move when one extreme value is added, so the fences stay where the bulk of the data is. You should not remove outliers when they are genuine and the model must handle such cases, or when they are the thing you are looking for, as in fraud detection, where the rare cases are the target.
blocks.rubric: Check that you explained why quartiles are robust.

cards.q: Write the box-plot (IQR) outlier rule.
cards.a: Outlier if x < Q1 − 1.5·IQR or x > Q3 + 1.5·IQR, with IQR = Q3 − Q1.

cards.q: What does each detector's fit_predict return for an outlier?
cards.a: −1 (inliers are +1).

cards.q: One line each: Isolation Forest, Elliptic Envelope, LOF, One-Class SVM.
cards.a: Few random splits isolate it; outside a robust Gaussian ellipse; lower density than its neighbours; outside a kernel boundary around the data (set nu).

cards.q: Why can a z-score miss an outlier?
cards.a: Masking: the outlier inflates the mean and standard deviation used to judge it.

blocks.md:
## Why this matters

Models only see numbers, and *how* a feature is turned into numbers often matters more than which model you pick. Distance-based models (KNN, SVM, k-means) and gradient descent need features on comparable scales; linear models need categories encoded so they do not invent a false order; skewed features can hide a simple relationship. The handbook covers the classical tools (scaling, dummy variables) and Sigmoid's own library, imperio (Box-Cox, ZCA, frequency and target encoding). This lesson explains each, with the sklearn equivalents, and how to apply them without leaking information.

## The transformer interface

Every sklearn transformer (and every imperio transformer) has the same three methods:

- `fit(X, y=None)`: learn what the transformation needs from the data (means, minimums, categories) and store it.
- `transform(X)`: apply the stored transformation.
- `fit_transform(X)`: both, on the same data.

The rule: **fit on the training set, transform both sets**. `scaler.fit_transform(X_train)` then `scaler.transform(X_test)`. (The handbook writes `fit_trainsform` twice; that typo raises an `AttributeError`.) Putting transformers in a `Pipeline` enforces the rule automatically, including inside cross-validation.

## Scaling numeric features

Gradient descent on unscaled features zig-zags: with height in metres and weight in kilograms, the cost surface is a long narrow valley, and a learning rate that suits one weight is too large or too small for the other. Distances are dominated by the largest-range feature. Trees and forests do not care, because they split on order.

For the values 2, 4, 6, 8, 100:

| scaler | formula | result |
|---|---|---|
| `StandardScaler` | (x − mean)/std | −0.578, −0.526, −0.473, −0.420, 1.997 |
| `MinMaxScaler` | (x − min)/(max − min) | 0, 0.020, 0.041, 0.061, 1 |
| `RobustScaler` | (x − median)/IQR | −1, −0.5, 0, 0.5, 23.5 |
| `MaxAbsScaler` | x / max(abs(x)) | 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 1 |

**Standardisation** gives each feature mean 0 and standard deviation 1. (The handbook describes it as bringing data "between −3 and 3"; there is no such bound, the 100 above could just as well be 1000. Most values of a roughly normal feature fall in that range.) **Normalisation** (min-max) squeezes values into [0, 1], which suits methods that need non-negative input such as multinomial naive Bayes; one outlier squashes everything else toward 0, as in the table. **RobustScaler** uses the median and IQR, so the outlier does not distort the other values. **MaxAbsScaler** keeps zeros at zero, useful for sparse data. Your drill `d-scale` implements three of them.

## Encoding categorical features

### Why not just number the categories?

Coding red = 0, green = 1, blue = 2 tells a linear model that blue is "twice green" and that green lies between red and blue. Unless the categories really are ordered (small < medium < large, which `OrdinalEncoder` handles), this invents structure that is not there.

### Dummy variables (one-hot encoding)

Create one 0/1 column per category, with a 1 in the column of the row's category:

| colour | green | red |
|---|---|---|
| red | 0 | 1 |
| green | 1 | 0 |
| blue | 0 | 0 |
| green | 1 | 0 |

That table is `pd.get_dummies(colours, drop_first=True, dtype=int)`: the columns are sorted (blue, green, red) and the first, blue, is dropped. Blue is now the **reference category**, represented by all zeros.

Why drop one? With an intercept, the full set of dummy columns always sums to 1, exactly equal to the intercept's column of ones. That is **perfect multicollinearity**, the **dummy variable trap**: the coefficients have no unique solution, so one of them is arbitrary. (The handbook says the trap breaks the assumption that observations are independent; it is the columns, not the observations, that become dependent.) Dropping one dummy fixes it, and each remaining coefficient means "difference from the reference category". Regularised models and trees cope with all k columns, so dropping is mainly a linear-regression concern.

In a pipeline, prefer sklearn's `OneHotEncoder`, which remembers the training categories:

```
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
enc = OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False).fit(train[["city"]])
enc.transform(test[["city"]])          # a city never seen in training becomes all zeros
```

`pd.get_dummies` applied separately to train and test can produce different columns if a category is missing from one of them.

One-hot is fine for a handful of categories (the handbook suggests fewer than ten); with hundreds it creates many sparse columns.

### Frequency encoding

Replace each category with its share of the rows. If A is 50% of the column, B 20% and C 30%, A → 0.5, B → 0.2, C → 0.3. (The handbook's text says B is 30%, but its own table, with A five times, B twice and C three times in ten rows, gives B 0.2 and C 0.3.) It produces one column regardless of the number of categories. Its weakness is **collision**: two categories with the same frequency become indistinguishable. imperio: `FrequencyImputationTransformer`.

### Target encoding

Replace each category with the mean of the target for that category (regression) or the share of the positive class (classification). In the handbook's example, category A's targets 100, 240, 130, 200, 100 average 154, B's 500 and 600 average 550, C's 30, 20, 40 average 30. One column, and very informative, but **dangerous**: the encoding is computed from the target, so a category seen only once gets exactly its own target value and the model learns to trust it. Compute it on training data only, ideally out-of-fold, and shrink rare categories toward the overall mean (smoothing). sklearn 1.3 and later has `TargetEncoder`, which does both; imperio: `TargetImputationTransformer`.

## Transforming distributions

### Log and Box-Cox

Many real features are right-skewed (incomes, prices, counts): most values small, a long tail of large ones. A log transform compresses the tail. The **Box-Cox** transformation generalises it with a parameter λ (lambda):

$$
y(λ) = (y^λ − 1) / λ   if λ ≠ 0
y(λ) = log(y)          if λ = 0
$$

λ = 1 only shifts the data, λ = 0.5 is a square-root type transform, λ = 0 is the log. Box-Cox requires **strictly positive** values; the **Yeo-Johnson** variant handles zero and negative values. For values 1, 2, 4, 8, 16: λ = 0 gives 0, 0.693, 1.386, 2.079, 2.773 (evenly spaced, because each value doubles); λ = 0.5 gives 0, 0.828, 2, 3.657, 6.

sklearn's `PowerTransformer(method="box-cox")` (or the default `"yeo-johnson"`) estimates the best λ from the training data. For 1,000 log-normal values (skewness 3.17), it estimates λ ≈ −0.012, essentially a log, and the skewness drops to 0.0. imperio's `BoxCoxTransformer` uses a fixed `l=0.5` by default instead of estimating it.

### ZCA whitening

**Whitening** transforms the features so they are uncorrelated and each has variance 1. PCA whitening rotates the data onto its principal components and rescales them; **ZCA** (zero-phase component analysis; the handbook calls it "zero component analysis") then rotates back, so the whitened features stay as close as possible to the originals. It removes multicollinearity, which can help linear models. imperio: `ZCATransformer`.

### Other ideas

- **Binning**: turn a numeric feature into ranges (`pd.cut`, `KBinsDiscretizer`), useful when the effect is a step.
- **Interactions and polynomials**: x₁·x₂, x² (`PolynomialFeatures`) let linear models fit curves.
- **Domain features**: body mass index from height and weight; day of week from a date; ratios such as debt/income. These often help more than any automatic method.

## Putting it together

```
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder, PowerTransformer
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), PowerTransformer(), StandardScaler()), num_cols),
    ("cat", make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent"), OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")), cat_cols),
])
model = make_pipeline(pre, LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)).fit(X_train, y_train)
```

`ColumnTransformer` applies a different pipeline to each list of columns and joins the results. Every statistic is learned from `X_train` only. For homework 15 to 17, record the test score before and after each transformation, and remember that a change of one or two test rows is noise: cross-validate when the difference is small. (The handbook reports Pima accuracy rising from 0.72 to 0.77 with Box-Cox and to 0.83 with ZCA, each on one split.)

## Common mistakes

> **Fitting a scaler or encoder on all data before splitting.** Test statistics leak into training.

> **Target encoding without out-of-fold estimates.** Rare categories memorise the target.

> **Box-Cox on zeros or negatives.** Use Yeo-Johnson or shift the data.

## Summary

Fit transformers on training data and transform both sets, ideally in a Pipeline. Standardise (mean 0, std 1) for gradient descent and distances; min-max into [0, 1]; RobustScaler for outliers. One-hot encode unordered categories and drop one dummy for unregularised linear models (the dummy trap is perfect multicollinearity). Frequency encoding uses category shares (collisions possible); target encoding uses the target mean per category (leakage risk; smooth and compute out-of-fold). Box-Cox (positive values) and Yeo-Johnson reduce skew; ZCA whitening removes correlations.

blocks.q:
MinMaxScaler is fitted on training values 10, 20, 30. What does it output for a test value of 35? Type a decimal.
```python
lo, hi = 10, 30
print((35 - lo) / (hi - lo))
```
blocks.why: The scaler keeps the training min and max, so new data can fall outside [0, 1]. That is correct behaviour, not a bug.

blocks.q: Why does a linear regression with an intercept and all k dummy columns of one category fail to have unique coefficients?
options: The dummy columns are not numeric
The k columns always sum to 1, duplicating the intercept column (perfect multicollinearity)
Observations become dependent on each other
blocks.why: Drop one dummy (drop_first=True); it becomes the reference category.

blocks.q:
Box-Cox with λ = 0.5 transforms y into (y^0.5 − 1)/0.5. What is the result for y = 9?
```python
print((9 ** 0.5 - 1) / 0.5)
```
blocks.why: (3 − 1)/0.5 = 4. With λ = 0 the transform would be log(9) ≈ 2.197.

blocks.q: A "city" column has 800 distinct values. Which encoding is the most practical for a linear model, if done carefully?
options: Target encoding with smoothing, computed out-of-fold on the training data
Dropping every row with a rare city
blocks.why: One-hot becomes huge and sparse; integer labels invent an order. Target encoding compresses the information into one column, as long as it does not leak.

blocks.q: Write `freq_encode(train, test)`: compute each category's share in `train` (rounded to 3) and return the encoded test list, using 0 for categories never seen in training. Then `target_encode(cats, ys)` returning a dict from category to the mean target for that category, rounded to 3.
blocks.why: These reproduce the handbook's tables. A category unseen in training gets 0 here; sklearn's TargetEncoder would use the overall target mean instead.

blocks.q: Which scaler is least affected by a single extreme value?
blocks.why: It centres on the median and divides by the IQR; one outlier does not move either.

blocks.q: From memory, explain how target encoding works, why it can leak the target, and two ways to make it safe.
blocks.model: Target encoding replaces each category with the mean of the target among the training rows in that category (for classification, the share of the positive class). It leaks because the encoded value is computed from the very targets the model is trained to predict: a category that appears once gets exactly its own target, so the model learns that the feature is perfectly predictive and fails on new data. To make it safe, compute the encoding only on training data and out-of-fold, so each row's value comes from other rows, and smooth rare categories toward the global mean. sklearn's TargetEncoder does both.
blocks.rubric: Check you mentioned training-only fitting.

cards.q: Write the standardisation and min-max formulas.
cards.a: (x − mean)/std; (x − min)/(max − min).

cards.q: What is the dummy variable trap?
cards.a: With an intercept, all k dummies sum to 1 and duplicate the intercept column (perfect multicollinearity); drop one.

cards.q: Write the Box-Cox transformation.
cards.a: (y^λ − 1)/λ for λ ≠ 0, log y for λ = 0; y must be positive (Yeo-Johnson handles any sign).

cards.q: What is frequency encoding's weakness, and target encoding's?
cards.a: Frequency: categories with equal frequency collide. Target: leaks the target unless fitted out-of-fold and smoothed.

lessons.title: Feature selection: filters, p-values and LASSO

blocks.md:
## Why this matters

More features are not always better. Irrelevant features add noise the model can overfit to, make distance-based models worse (in many dimensions all points look far apart), slow training (the handbook's complexity table: almost every algorithm's cost grows with the number of features d) and make the model harder to explain. Feature selection keeps the columns that carry information about the target. The handbook teaches four methods through Sigmoid's library kydavra; this lesson explains what each computes, adds the sklearn equivalents, and warns about the most common way selection inflates scores.

## Three families

- **Filter methods** score each feature on its own, against the target, before any model: correlation, point-biserial correlation, the ANOVA F-test, chi-squared, mutual information. Fast; blind to interactions between features.
- **Wrapper methods** train a model on different subsets and keep the best: backward elimination by p-value, recursive feature elimination (`RFE`), sequential selection (`SequentialFeatureSelector`). Better at capturing interactions; slower.
- **Embedded methods** select as part of training: LASSO sets weights to exactly zero; tree models provide importances (`SelectFromModel`).

Remember that selection works on columns as the model sees them: after one-hot encoding, a category becomes several columns, and dropping one of them changes the reference category rather than removing the feature. Selecting whole groups of dummies together is usually what you want.

## P-value feature selection (regression)

A linear regression fitted with statsmodels' `OLS` reports, for each coefficient, a **p-value** for the **null hypothesis** that the true coefficient is 0 (the feature has no linear effect once the other features are in the model).

The p-value is the probability, *assuming the null hypothesis is true*, of getting an estimate at least as far from 0 as the one observed. A small p-value (below the **significance level** α, usually 0.05) means the data would be surprising if the feature had no effect, so we keep it. A large p-value means the data are compatible with no effect; it does not prove the feature is useless, and it says nothing direct about production performance (the handbook's informal reading). p-values also depend on the other features in the model and on the sample size.

kydavra's `PValueSelector` performs **backward elimination**:

1. Fit OLS with all features.
2. Find the feature with the largest p-value.
3. If that p-value is below α, stop; otherwise remove the feature and go back to 1.

On sklearn's diabetes data (442 patients, 10 features, target = disease progression), backward elimination with α = 0.05 removes, in order: age (p = 0.867), s3 (0.639), s6 (0.304) and s4 (0.262). It keeps sex, bmi, bp, s1, s2 and s5, all with p < 0.05, while the adjusted R² stays at about 0.508. Four features dropped, no fit lost.

```
import statsmodels.api as sm
model = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(X[cols])).fit()   # add_constant adds the intercept column
model.pvalues                                         # one p-value per coefficient
```

Notice that s2 had a large p-value early on and became significant once s4 was removed: s1, s2 and s4 are correlated blood measurements, and correlated features share and blur each other's evidence. Removing one at a time, rather than all large p-values at once, is why the algorithm loops.

## LASSO selection (regression)

LASSO is linear regression with an **L1 penalty**:

$$
cost = (1/n) Σ_i (y_i − ŷ_i)² + α Σ_j |w_j|
$$

The penalty α Σ|wⱼ| charges for the absolute size of every weight. Unlike the squared L2 penalty of Ridge, which shrinks weights toward 0 but rarely to exactly 0, the L1 penalty's constant pull drives weak features' weights **exactly to zero**. The larger α, the more weights reach zero. Features must be standardised first, or the penalty treats them unequally.

Standardised diabetes data with sklearn's `Lasso` (whose cost uses 1/(2n) in front of the squared errors, so its α values are on a different scale from the formula above):

| α | non-zero weights | kept features |
|---|---|---|
| 0.1 | 9 | all but s3 |
| 1 | 7 | sex, bmi, bp, s1, s3, s5, s6 |
| 5 | 5 | sex, bmi, bp, s3, s5 |
| 10 | 4 | bmi, bp, s3, s5 |
| 20 | 3 | bmi, bp, s5 |

bmi, bp and s5 survive the strongest penalty: they are the most informative. kydavra's `LassoSelector` searches α between `alpha_start` and `alpha_finish` for the lowest error and keeps features whose weight is not below 10^−power. In sklearn, `LassoCV` picks α by cross-validation (here α ≈ 0.079, keeping 9 features: the best-predicting α is often mild), and `SelectFromModel(Lasso(alpha=...))` turns any α into a selector.

## Correlation selection

**Pearson correlation** r = cov(x, y)/(σₓ σ_y) measures linear association, from −1 to +1. kydavra's `PearsonCorrelationSelector` keeps features whose absolute correlation with the target lies between `min_corr` (0.5) and `max_corr` (0.8): weak features are dropped, and suspiciously strong ones are dropped too, because a near-perfect correlation with the target often means a **leak** (a column computed from the target or recorded after it). With `erase_corr=True` it also drops features highly correlated with each other (multicollinearity: they carry the same information). On the diabetes data only bmi (0.586) and s5 (0.566) pass the 0.5 threshold, a much stricter cut than p-values or LASSO.

**Spearman** correlation is Pearson on ranks, capturing any monotonic relationship; **Kendall** counts concordant pairs. Both are more robust to outliers.

## Point-biserial correlation (binary classification)

When the target is 0/1 and the feature continuous, the **point-biserial correlation** is:

$$
r_pb = (M₁ − M₀) / s · √(n₁ n₀ / n²)
$$

M₁ and M₀ are the feature's means in class 1 and class 0, s the feature's standard deviation (dividing by n), n₁ and n₀ the class sizes and n the total. It equals the Pearson correlation computed with the 0/1 labels as numbers. The handbook writes M₀ − M₁, which only flips the sign; selectors use the absolute value.

Example: feature values 2, 3, 3, 4 in class 0 and 5, 6, 6, 7 in class 1. M₀ = 3, M₁ = 6, s ≈ 1.658, √(4·4/64) = 0.5, so r_pb = 3/1.658 × 0.5 ≈ 0.905: a strongly separating feature. kydavra's `PointBiserialCorrSelector` groups features into correlation bands of width 0.1 and keeps the top `last_level` bands, which makes it one of the strictest selectors.

## Selection without fooling yourself

If you choose features using all the data and then cross-validate, the selection has already seen the validation folds: with enough random features, some will correlate with the target by chance, and the score will be optimistic. Do selection inside the pipeline so it is refitted in every fold:

```
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SelectKBest(f_classif, k=5), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
cross_val_score(pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=5).mean()
```

kydavra's `select(df, "target")` takes a whole DataFrame; call it on the training part only, then keep the same columns for the test set.

For homework 16, report the test metric with all features and with each selector's subset, plus the number of features kept: a selector that keeps 4 of 13 features at the same accuracy is a real gain.

## Common mistakes

> **Reading a large p-value as "useless".** It means "no evidence of a linear effect given the other features".

> **Selecting on the full dataset.** Selection is part of training.

> **Keeping a feature with correlation 0.99 to the target.** Check it is not a leak.

## Summary

Filters score features one at a time (Pearson, Spearman, point-biserial, F-test, mutual information); wrappers search subsets with a model (p-value backward elimination, RFE); embedded methods select while training (LASSO, tree importances). Backward elimination removes the largest p-value until all are below α. LASSO's L1 penalty α Σ|w| sets weak weights exactly to zero; scale first. Point-biserial r = (M₁ − M₀)/s · √(n₁n₀/n²) equals Pearson with 0/1 labels. Always select inside the training data or pipeline.

blocks.q: What does a p-value of 0.80 for a regression coefficient tell you?
options: The feature explains 80% of the target
There is an 80% chance the feature is useless
If the true coefficient were 0, an estimate this far from 0 would be very common, so there is no evidence of an effect
blocks.why: The p-value is computed assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

blocks.q:
Class 0 has feature values 2, 3, 3, 4 and class 1 has 5, 6, 6, 7. What is the point-biserial correlation, rounded to 3?
```python
x = [2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7]
m = sum(x) / 8
s = (sum((v - m) ** 2 for v in x) / 8) ** 0.5
print(round((6 - 3) / s * (4 * 4 / 64) ** 0.5, 3))
```
Why does LASSO produce exactly-zero weights while Ridge usually does not?
options: The L1 penalty's pull on a weight does not weaken as the weight approaches 0, so weak weights are pushed all the way to 0
Ridge does not use a penalty
LASSO removes features with large p-values
blocks.why: Ridge's squared penalty has a gradient 2αw that vanishes near 0, so weights shrink but rarely reach it; L1's gradient stays α·sign(w).

blocks.q: A feature has correlation 0.99 with the target. What should you do first?
options: Check whether it leaks the target (computed from it or recorded after it)
blocks.why: Real predictors are rarely that perfect. kydavra's max_corr default of 0.8 exists for this reason.

blocks.q: Write `backward_eliminate(pvals_by_step, alpha)`: you get a function `pvals_by_step(cols)` that returns a dict of p-values for the given columns. Starting from all its columns (call it with `None` first to get them), repeatedly remove the column with the largest p-value while that p-value is ≥ alpha. Return `(kept_sorted, removed_in_order)`.
blocks.starter:
def backward_eliminate(pvals_by_step, alpha):
    pass
blocks.solution:
def backward_eliminate(pvals_by_step, alpha):
    cols = list(pvals_by_step(None))
    removed = []
    while cols:
        p = pvals_by_step(cols)
        worst = max(cols, key=lambda c: p[c])
        if p[worst] < alpha:
            break
        cols.remove(worst)
        removed.append(worst)
    return sorted(cols), removed
blocks.why: The fake p-value table mimics the diabetes example: s1 and s2 only become significant once their correlated partner s4 has gone, which is why the algorithm refits after every removal instead of dropping all large p-values at once.

blocks.q: You pick the 10 features most correlated with the target on the whole dataset, then report 5-fold cross-validation accuracy. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, correlation is a filter method
The selection used the validation folds, so the score is optimistically biased
Correlation cannot be used for classification
blocks.why: Put the selector inside a Pipeline so it is refitted on the training folds only.

blocks.q: From memory, describe backward elimination by p-values and LASSO selection, and give one advantage of each.
blocks.model: Backward elimination fits an OLS regression with all features, finds the feature whose coefficient has the largest p-value, and removes it if that p-value is at least the significance level, usually 0.05; it refits and repeats until every remaining p-value is below the threshold. Its advantage is that it is easy to explain statistically and refitting after each removal handles correlated features fairly. LASSO adds the penalty alpha times the sum of absolute weights to the squared error, which drives the weights of weak features exactly to zero; features with zero weight are dropped. Its advantage is that selection happens in one model fit and alpha can be tuned by cross-validation for prediction quality.
blocks.rubric: Check that you mentioned refitting after each removal and standardising before LASSO.

cards.q: Name the three families of feature selection with one example each.
cards.a: Filter (correlation, F-test), wrapper (backward elimination, RFE), embedded (LASSO, tree importances).

cards.q: Write the LASSO cost function.
cards.a: (1/n) Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)² + α Σ|wⱼ|.

cards.q: What is a p-value?
cards.a: The probability, assuming the null hypothesis (no effect) is true, of a result at least as extreme as observed.

cards.q: Write the point-biserial correlation.
cards.a: r = (M₁ − M₀)/s · √(n₁n₀/n²), the Pearson correlation with 0/1 labels.
